clinicalPearls: Cardinal features are fatigable, fluctuating skeletal muscle weakness that worsens with repeated use or late in the day and improves with rest or sleep (Harrison 22e p.3625-3626).

Ocular and eyelid muscles are commonly involved early; diplopia and ptosis are frequent initial symptoms, and facial weakness can produce a 'snarling' expression on attempted smiling (Harrison 22e p.3626).
Bulbar involvement causes nasal/dysarthric 'mushy' speech, dysphagia with nasal regurgitation or aspiration, and chewing weakness; neck extensor weakness can cause head drop (Harrison 22e p.3626).
If weakness stays confined to ocular muscles for 3 years, later generalization is unlikely (ocular MG), though rare patients generalize beyond 5 years (Harrison 22e p.3626).
Bulbar, neck, and ventilatory weakness can be especially prominent in MuSK antibody-positive MG (Harrison 22e p.3626).

Ice-pack test: applying ice over a ptotic eye for 2 min produces a lid rise of 2 mm or more (positive) when ptosis is due to an NMJ defect; it is a quick, very sensitive bedside test (Harrison 22e p.3626-3627).
Approximately 10-15% of MG patients have a thymoma, so chest CT or MRI to evaluate the thymus is performed at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3628).
harrison.pathophysiology: MG is an autoimmune NMJ disorder in which the number of available postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) is reduced and the postsynaptic folds are flattened ('simplified'), decreasing the efficiency of neuromuscular transmission so that normally released ACh produces small end-plate potentials that may fail to trigger muscle action potentials. Anti-AChR antibodies (IgG, T-cell dependent) act by three mechanisms: accelerated AChR turnover via cross-linking and endocytosis, complement-mediated damage to the postsynaptic membrane, and blockade of the ACh-binding site. Anti-MuSK antibodies (IgG4, do not activate complement) impair MuSK-LRP4 interaction and AChR clustering; anti-LRP4 antibodies (IgG1) cause complement-mediated destruction. The normal decline in ACh release on repeated activity (presynaptic rundown) combined with reduced transmission efficiency produces myasthenic fatigue and the decremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation. The thymus is abnormal in ~75% of AChR antibody-positive patients (~65% hyperplastic, ~10% thymoma) (Harrison 22e p.3624-3626).
additionalDifferentials: Congenital myasthenic syndromes (nonautoimmune, >30 genes; double-seronegative MG mimic)
Immune checkpoint inhibitor-related autoimmune MG (and ICI-related myositis/myocarditis mimic)
Intracranial mass compressing extraocular nerves (e.g., sphenoid ridge meningioma)
Progressive external ophthalmoplegia / mitochondrial myopathy (Kearns-Sayre syndrome)
infectionMimics: Botulism (Clostridium botulinum toxin cleaves proteins needed for ACh release, causing myasthenia-like bulbar weakness without sensory signs; reflexes present early)
nonInfectiousMimics: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (presynaptic, P/Q-type calcium channel antibodies)
additionalInvestigations: Anti-AChR antibody radioimmunoassay (positive in ~85% of generalized MG, ~50% of ocular MG; a positive result is virtually diagnostic but a negative result does not exclude MG)
Anti-MuSK antibodies (present in up to ~40% of AChR antibody-negative generalized MG)
Anti-LRP4 antibodies (low specificity; only tested when phenotype/electrodiagnostics fit MG but AChR and MuSK antibodies are absent)
Repetitive nerve stimulation (decrement >10% at 2-3 Hz is highly probable for MG)
Single-fiber EMG (blocking and jitter with normal fiber density; sensitive and confirmatory but not specific)
Chest CT or MRI to evaluate the thymus for thymoma
Thyroid function tests in all patients with suspected MG
CT or MRI of head/orbits to exclude intracranial lesions in ocular or cranial presentations
Pulmonary function tests / forced vital capacity to assess respiratory impairment
redFlags: Myasthenic crisis: ventilatory weakness requiring intubation or noninvasive ventilation to avoid intubation, managed in intensive care (treat respiratory infection, attend to fluids); requires rescue therapy with IVIg or plasmapheresis (Harrison 22e p.3626, p.3628-3629).
Dysphagia with nasal regurgitation or aspiration of liquids/food (bulbar involvement) (Harrison 22e p.3626).
Enlargement of the thymus in a patient older than 40 years is highly suspicious for thymoma (Harrison 22e p.3628).
Infection or tapering of MG therapy can precipitate myasthenic exacerbation or crisis (Harrison 22e p.3626).
ICI-related MG with concurrent myocarditis carries a high fatality rate in fulminant disease (Harrison 22e p.3627).
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis has improved strikingly with modern treatment, and nearly all myasthenic patients can be returned to full productive lives with proper therapy. The course is variable, with exacerbations and remissions, particularly in the first 1-3 years; in ~85% of patients weakness becomes generalized. A cure remains elusive (Harrison 22e p.3625-3628).
pitfalls: A negative anti-AChR antibody test does not exclude MG, and the antibody level does not correlate well with disease severity (Harrison 22e p.3627).

Distinguish LEMS from MG: LEMS is presynaptic (P/Q-type calcium channel antibodies), preferentially affects proximal lower-limb muscles, typically spares prominent ocular/bulbar onset, and shows depressed/absent reflexes plus autonomic features (dry mouth, orthostasis, impotence); unlike MG, strength and CMAP amplitude increase (incremental response) after brief exercise or high-rate (20-50 Hz) stimulation. In older adults LEMS is associated with malignancy, most commonly small-cell lung cancer (Harrison 22e p.3628).
Anti-striated muscle (titin) antibodies are not pathogenic and do not confirm MG or a thymoma (Harrison 22e p.3627).

Aminoglycoside, quinolone, and macrolide antibiotics, IV magnesium, procainamide, and penicillamine can exacerbate myasthenic weakness; botulinum toxin injections should be avoided in MG patients (Harrison 22e p.3627).

Anti-MuSK MG generally responds less to anticholinesterase agents (and may worsen) and does not respond to complement inhibition because MuSK antibodies are IgG4 and do not activate complement (Harrison 22e p.3626, p.3628-3629).
Diagnosis must be confirmed definitively before treatment because other treatable conditions mimic MG and treatment carries surgical/drug risks (Harrison 22e p.3626).
harrison.severityClassification: Weakness is classified as ocular versus generalized (the latter affecting facial, bulbar, axial, or limb muscles in ~85% of patients). Worsening requiring intubation or noninvasive ventilation defines myasthenic crisis; all other worsening is termed exacerbation. Standardized measures referenced include the Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living (MGADL) and Quantitative MG (QMG) scores (Harrison 22e p.3626, p.3631).
management: Symptomatic treatment with the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor pyridostigmine to improve neuromuscular transmission

Immunosuppression with corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents such as azathioprine or mycophenolate for generalised disease, with targeted therapies (complement inhibitors such as eculizumab, or neonatal-Fc-receptor antagonists) for refractory disease
Thymectomy for thymoma and in appropriate AChR-antibody-positive generalised myasthenia to improve long-term outcomes
Rapid immunotherapy with plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin for myasthenic crisis and severe exacerbations
Airway protection and ventilatory support in intensive care for myasthenic crisis with respiratory or bulbar failure
Avoid or use cautiously drugs that worsen transmission, including aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium and certain beta-blockers, and treat intercurrent infection promptly as a crisis trigger
Screen for and manage associated autoimmune disease, particularly thyroid, noting MuSK-antibody disease responds less well to anticholinesterases and often favours rituximab
